title: Data Structures & Algorithms
description: Choose data structures and algorithms using their preconditions, invariants and costs. Practise graph traversal, greedy reasoning and dynamic programming in tested projects.
prerequisites: Complete Python variables, loops, functions and collections first, or translate the examples into a language you know.
You only need arithmetic and a willingness to trace a few steps on paper.
setup: Examples use Python 3 and its standard library. Save them in a .py file and run python filename.py (or py filename.py on Windows).
Download algorithms.py to run the binary search, BFS and dynamic-programming examples with assertions. No packages or network access are required.
Before running code, predict the output and identify empty, one-element, duplicate and missing-value cases.
outcomes: Describe time and auxiliary-space growth under stated assumptions.
Choose arrays, maps, stacks, queues, heaps and graph representations.
Trace binary search and traversal invariants.
Build and test a small shortest-hop learning-prerequisite explorer.
nextSteps: Study balanced trees, union-find and string algorithms.
Explore Bellman–Ford, all-pairs paths and network flow.
Deepen amortized analysis, randomized algorithms and formal proofs.

downloads.title: Independent graph and knapsack oracle tests
Worked advanced algorithm reasoning and feedback

lessons.title: 1. Correctness before speed
lessons.takeaway: State the contract, then count how work grows.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: An algorithm is a procedure for solving a problem. Its contract says what inputs it accepts and what result it promises. Test a tiny example by hand before discussing speed.

Big-O describes an upper bound on growth, not a stopwatch reading. A single pass over n values has O(n) time if each step costs constant time. Auxiliary space counts extra storage, separately from the input.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Early exit can improve a particular run without changing the worst-case bound. State whether you mean best, average, expected or worst case.

exercise.prompt: Count comparisons for a missing target in [2,4,6]. Then write a version returning that count.
checks: Missing target takes three comparisons.
Empty input takes zero.
Worst case scales with the list length.

quiz.question: A full scan of n values has which typical time bound?
quiz.explanation: Each element is inspected once, assuming constant-cost comparisons.

lessons.title: 2. Arrays, lists and linked nodes
lessons.takeaway: Access patterns matter more than the name of a structure.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A Python list is a dynamic array of references. Index access is constant-time under the usual model. Inserting at the front shifts existing references and takes linear time.

A linked list stores references between nodes instead of adjacent index slots. Inserting after an already-known node can be constant-time, but finding that node may require a linear walk. Neither representation is universally faster.
sections.example:
values = [10, 20, 30]
print(values[1])  # 20
values.insert(0, 5)
print(values)     # [5, 10, 20, 30]

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Appending to a dynamic array is amortized O(1), not a promise that every individual append costs the same. Slicing copies selected references and uses extra memory.

sections.title: Amortized cost of appending
paragraphs: A dynamic array such as a Python list reserves spare capacity. When it is full, it allocates a larger block and copies every item, an O(n) step. Because capacity grows by a constant factor, those copies are rare: over n appends the total copying is less than 2n, so each append is O(1) amortized, meaning averaged over the whole sequence rather than guaranteed for every call.
Growing by a fixed amount instead, say 10 slots, makes n appends cost O(n²) in total. Amortized bounds also explain why a single append can occasionally be slow even though the average is constant.
sections.example:
capacity, size, copies = 1, 0, 0
for _ in range(1000):
    if size == capacity:
        copies += size   # move every item into a block twice as large
        capacity *= 2
    size += 1
print(size, capacity, copies, copies < 2 * size)

# Expected output:
# 1000 1024 1023 True

exercise.prompt: Reverse a list into a new list and explain the cost.
checks: Original list is unchanged.
Empty input returns an empty list.
Time O(n), extra space O(n).

quiz.question: Is insertion at the front of a Python list O(1)?
quiz.explanation: Front insertion moves references across the array, so its cost grows with n.

lessons.title: 3. Hash maps and sets
lessons.takeaway: Use a map for keyed information and a set for membership.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A dictionary associates keys with values; a set records unique membership. For well-behaved hashes, lookups have expected constant time, but collision behavior can worsen the cost. Hashing a long key itself may also cost time.
A frequency table is a natural dictionary problem. Store the count seen so far for each item rather than repeatedly scanning the entire list.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: A map can use more memory than a scan. Keys need valid hashing/equality behavior; Python lists are not dictionary keys.

exercise.prompt: Return the first repeated item, or None if no item repeats.
checks: Returns the first repetition in traversal order.
Expected O(n) time and O(n) extra space.
Contract: hashable items; None is the no-result sentinel.

quiz.question: Which structure fits unique membership?
quiz.explanation: A set directly models whether an item has been seen.

lessons.title: 4. Stacks and queues
lessons.takeaway: A stack removes the newest item; a queue removes the oldest.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A stack models last-in-first-out behavior such as undo. A queue models first-in-first-out behavior such as requests awaiting service. Name both ends explicitly when tracing operations.
Python list `append`/`pop` work well for a stack. Use `collections.deque` for removing from the front of a queue; repeatedly using `list.pop(0)` adds shifting work.
sections.example:
from collections import deque
queue = deque(['A', 'B'])
queue.append('C')
print(queue.popleft())  # A
stack = ['A', 'B']
print(stack.pop())      # B

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: A structure's ordering policy affects correctness as well as performance. Replacing a queue with a stack changes graph traversal order.

exercise.prompt: Check balanced round parentheses, rejecting an unmatched close immediately.
checks: Handles empty text as balanced.
Other characters are ignored by this contract.
One bracket type only; multiple types require a stack of opening brackets.

quiz.question: What leaves a FIFO queue first?
quiz.explanation: FIFO preserves insertion order when serving queued items.

lessons.title: 5. Binary search and invariants
lessons.takeaway: Discard half the candidates only when order justifies it.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: Binary search requires data sorted under the same comparison used by the search. Maintain inclusive low and high indexes. If the middle value is below the target, all values at or left of it can be excluded.

The invariant is: if the target exists and has not been found, it lies in the remaining range. Each update must shrink that range. This version returns any matching index, not necessarily the first duplicate.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Sorting an unsorted list first has a cost. For one search, a linear scan may be simpler; binary search is valuable when sorted data already exists or is reused.

exercise.prompt: Trace target 6 in [2,5,8,12,16], then test empty and one-element arrays.
exercise.solution:
# Using binary_search above:
assert binary_search([2, 5, 8, 12, 16], 6) == -1
assert binary_search([], 6) == -1
assert binary_search([6], 6) == 0
# Mid values: 8, 2, 5; then low > high.
checks: Every iteration shrinks the candidate interval.
Worst-case search time O(log n), auxiliary space O(1).
Duplicates may produce any matching index.

quiz.question: What precondition does this search require?
quiz.explanation: Sorted order makes it safe to discard a half-range.

frames.label: Start with all candidates
frames.explanation: low=0, high=4, mid=2. Since 8 < 12, indexes 0–2 can be discarded.

frames.label: Keep the upper half
frames.explanation: low=3, high=4, mid=3. The middle value equals the target.

frames.label: Return the matching index
frames.explanation: Two loop iterations found the target. The code performs three value comparisons: equality and less-than for 8, then equality for 12. Other searches can take more iterations.

lessons.title: 6. Sorting and stable order
lessons.takeaway: A comparison rule and tie policy are part of the result.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: Sorting enables grouped display, merging and efficient search. Python's `sorted` returns a new list; `list.sort` modifies the existing list. A key function expresses what should be compared.

A stable sort preserves the prior order of items with equal keys. This helps when records have ties. For general comparison sorting, O(n log n) is a common efficient bound; simple insertion sort has O(n²) worst-case time.
sections.example:
rows = [('SQL', 20), ('Python', 10), ('React', 20)]
print(sorted(rows, key=lambda row: row[1]))
# [('Python', 10), ('SQL', 20), ('React', 20)]

sections.title: Read a key function and a tie-break
paragraphs: `key` receives a function, not its result. `def duration(row): return row[1]` and `lambda row: row[1]` express the same key here. `sorted` calls that function for each row and orders by its returned value.

A tuple key compares its first position first, then later positions only on ties. For `(-priority, title)`, priority 3 gives -3 and sorts before priority 2 giving -2. Equal priorities then use title in ascending order. The original records are returned, not the key tuples.
sections.example:
def duration(row):
    return row[1]
rows = [("SQL", 20), ("Python", 10), ("React", 20)]
assert sorted(rows, key=duration) == sorted(rows, key=lambda row: row[1])

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Never benchmark only already-sorted tiny inputs and conclude an algorithm is best. Include reversed input, duplicates and representative sizes.

exercise.prompt: Sort tasks by descending priority, breaking ties by ascending title.
exercise.solution:
tasks = [('SQL', 2), ('React', 3), ('Python', 2)]
ordered = sorted(tasks, key=lambda task: (-task[1], task[0]))
assert ordered == [('React', 3), ('Python', 2), ('SQL', 2)]
checks: Priority 3 comes first.
Equal priority uses title.
Input order remains unchanged.

quiz.question: What does stable sorting preserve?
quiz.explanation: Stability specifies tie behavior, not that the entire order stays unchanged.

lessons.title: 7. Recursion, base cases and trees
lessons.takeaway: A recursive call must move toward a smaller problem.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: Recursion expresses a problem in terms of smaller instances. A base case stops expansion. A recursive algorithm can still consume substantial stack space even if its code is short.

A tree represents parent-child relationships without cycles. A recursive traversal can process a node and then its children. A highly skewed tree may have depth n; Python recursion has practical limits, so an explicit stack is often safer for deep input.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: This example assumes a real acyclic tree and well-formed records. A cycle would never reach a base case. Counting calls and maximum depth are different measurements.

sections.title: Implemented tree practice
paragraphs: The new binary-search-tree lesson and `trees_graphs.py` supply an actual search tree; compare its explicit stack with recursive traversal and its height-dependent costs.

exercise.prompt: Count nodes in the same tree format.
checks: Leaf returns one.
Each node is visited once: O(n) time.
Call-stack depth is O(h), where h is tree height.

quiz.question: What must every terminating recursive path reach?
quiz.explanation: Without a base case and progress toward it, recursion does not terminate.

lessons.title: 8. Implemented binary search tree: ordering and deletion
lessons.takeaway: An unbalanced BST preserves ordering; its cost depends on height.

sections.title: Connect a tree picture to node references
paragraphs: A node is a record containing a key and references to its left and right children. `None` means that child is absent. A class constructor uses `self` to attach these fields to the new object. Child references point to other nodes rather than copying their entire subtrees.

Before deletion, trace search only: compare with the current key, follow left for a smaller target or right for a larger one, and stop at equality or `None`. In the example, searching 7 visits 10 then 5 then `None`. The later linked-nodes lesson practises changing a single link before larger tree edits.
sections.example:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None
root = Node(10)
root.left = Node(5)
root.right = Node(20)
assert root.left.key == 5
assert root.left.right is None

sections.title: Contract and collaboration
paragraphs: The downloadable `trees_graphs.py` implements insert, contains, delete and inorder keys with integer keys (`bool` rejected). Every left subtree key is smaller and every right subtree key is larger than its ancestor. Duplicate insertion is a no-op; deleting a missing key returns `False`. Deletion of a two-child node copies the inorder successor and removes its original node, preserving a successor right child.

Operations are iterative. Search, insert and delete take O(h), worst O(n) in a skewed tree; inorder traversal takes O(n) with O(h) stack. There is no balancing guarantee. The exhaustive four-key insertion/deletion tests compare against a set and independently check global ancestor bounds after every mutation.

sections.title: Trace a two-child deletion
paragraphs: Insert 10, 5, 20, 15, 17 and 30. To delete root 10, find the smallest key in its right subtree: 15. Copy 15 into the root, then replace the original 15 link with its right child 17. Copying a key without removing its old node would introduce a duplicate; removing that node without reconnecting 17 would lose an entire subtree.
sections.example:
from trees_graphs import BinarySearchTree
tree = BinarySearchTree()
for key in [10, 5, 20, 15, 17, 30]:
    tree.insert(key)
assert tree.delete(10)
assert tree.keys() == [5, 15, 17, 20, 30]
assert not tree.insert(15)
assert not tree.delete(99)

sections.title: Verify the invariant beyond a sample
paragraphs: Use `test_trees_graphs.py` to compare every four-key insertion/deletion order against a set. Check global ancestor bounds, not only immediate parent-child comparisons: a misplaced descendant can satisfy its immediate parent while violating the root bound. The successor-with-right-child fixture tests the splice above. Sorted insertion creates a chain; iterative traversal avoids recursion failure but does not improve that chain's linear search cost.

sections.title: Why search trees need balancing
paragraphs: Search, insertion and deletion in a binary search tree cost O(h) for a tree of height h. Inserting already sorted keys builds a chain where h = n; random insertion order gives a height close to the O(log n) of a balanced tree, but real data is often sorted.

Self-balancing trees repair the shape after each change with local rotations. AVL trees keep subtree heights within one of each other; red-black trees allow a little more imbalance in exchange for fewer rotations. Databases use B-trees, whose wide nodes hold many keys per disk page. Python has no built-in balanced tree: use a `dict` for exact lookups and `bisect` on a sorted list for ordered queries.
sections.example:
import random

def bst_height(values):
    def insert(node, value):
        if node is None:
            return [value, None, None]
        side = 1 if value < node[0] else 2
        node[side] = insert(node[side], value)
        return node

    def height(node):
        return 0 if node is None else 1 + max(height(node[1]), height(node[2]))

    root = None
    for value in values:
        root = insert(root, value)
    return height(root)

n = 127
ordered = list(range(n))
shuffled = ordered[:]
random.Random(4).shuffle(shuffled)
print("sorted inserts:", bst_height(ordered))
print("random inserts:", bst_height(shuffled))
print("balanced:", n.bit_length())

# Expected output:
# sorted inserts: 127
# random inserts: 13
# balanced: 7

exercise.prompt: Predict the root deletion for [10,5,20,15,17,30]. Run tests, then explain how successor 15 keeps right child 17. Compare sorted insertion with a balanced insertion order.
exercise.solution: Inorder after deleting 10 is [5,15,17,20,30]. The successor is detached from its old parent by replacing that link with its right child. Run python -m unittest -v test_trees_graphs.py.

Duplicate and missing-key policies are tested.
Skewed input costs O(n), not guaranteed O(log n).

Check only that the root has a left and a right child.
Check only one insertion sequence with no deletions.
quiz.explanation: A set provides the expected membership. Checking each node against its permitted range catches ordering errors below the root.

lessons.title: 9. Graphs and breadth-first search
lessons.takeaway: Use a queue to explore unweighted shortest paths by layers.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A graph stores vertices and edges. Unlike a tree, it can contain cycles and multiple routes. An adjacency list maps each vertex to its neighbors; directed edges have a direction.

Breadth-first search discovers vertices in increasing edge distance from the start. Mark a vertex seen when enqueuing it, not after repeated enqueues. It finds shortest paths by number of edges in an unweighted graph, not cheapest routes with arbitrary weights.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: A seen set prevents cycles from causing repeated traversal. With adjacency lists and expected constant-time hashing, traversal is O(V+E) over reachable vertices/edges.

sections.title: Changing the question changes the algorithm
paragraphs: A has a direct edge to B costing nine and an edge to C costing one; C reaches B for one more. BFS reports one hop to B, correctly answering fewest edges. It does not choose the cheapest two-edge route. Before tracing a queue, say whether you minimize hops, weight, elapsed time or some other quantity.

The method-selection lab runs both BFS and Dijkstra on this same graph. An unreachable Z is absent from both reachable-distance maps. Reporting zero for Z would confuse unreachable with the legitimate zero distance from A to itself. Use the result representation to preserve that distinction.

exercise.prompt: Add an unreachable node D and explain its result.
exercise.solution:
graph = {'A':['B'], 'B':['C'], 'C':['A'], 'D':[]}
result = distances(graph, 'A')
assert 'D' not in result
# Absence means unreachable, not distance zero.
checks: Cycles terminate.
Start has distance zero.
Unreachable vertices are omitted.

quiz.question: When does ordinary BFS give shortest path distances?
options: For unweighted edges measured in hop count
quiz.explanation: Queue layers correspond to increasing numbers of edges, not arbitrary weights.

lessons.title: 10. Heaps and priority queues
lessons.takeaway: A heap efficiently exposes an extreme, not a fully sorted sequence.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: A min-heap keeps the smallest element at its root. In Python `heapq` operates on a list. Pushing or popping has logarithmic time in heap size; reading the minimum has constant time when nonempty.

A scheduler can use (priority, sequence, task) entries. A sequence number provides a defined tie-breaker and avoids comparing task objects when priorities tie. Real schedulers also need cancellation and fairness policies.
sections.example:
import heapq
heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, (2, 0, 'SQL'))
heapq.heappush(heap, (1, 1, 'Python'))
print(heapq.heappop(heap)[2])  # Python

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Iteration over the underlying heap list is not guaranteed sorted order. Repeated popping sorts the extracted sequence but consumes the heap.

exercise.prompt: Add React at priority 1 with sequence 2. Predict the pop order.
exercise.solution:
import heapq
heap = [(2, 0, 'SQL'), (1, 1, 'Python'), (1, 2, 'React')]
heapq.heapify(heap)
order = [heapq.heappop(heap)[2] for _ in range(3)]
assert order == ['Python', 'React', 'SQL']
checks: Smaller priority values are served first here.
Sequence resolves equal priority.
Check for an empty heap before popping.

quiz.question: Is the entire heap list sorted?
options: No, only the heap ordering invariant is guaranteed
quiz.explanation: The smallest is at the root; siblings and subtrees are not globally sorted.

lessons.title: 11. Dynamic programming
lessons.takeaway: Reuse solutions to overlapping subproblems with a clearly defined state.

sections.title: Concept
paragraphs: Dynamic programming stores answers to repeated subproblems. Define what each state means before writing a recurrence. For ways to climb n steps using moves of one or two, ways(n)=ways(n−1)+ways(n−2).

Set ways(0)=1 for the empty sequence and ways(1)=1. The iterative version retains only two prior counts. It uses O(n) additions and a constant number of integer variables; exact large-integer arithmetic still grows as the result gets larger.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Memoization is not a substitute for a valid recurrence. Test base cases separately. A greedy choice needs a proof; it does not follow from having a short implementation.

sections.title: Derive a second recurrence rather than memorising stairs
paragraphs: For unlimited coins of values 1, 3 and 4, define best[a] as the minimum coin count for amount a. The last coin c leaves amount a-c, so each reachable best[a-c]+1 is a candidate. Start best[0]=0; represent unreachable amounts with `None`, not zero. At six, using three after three yields two coins, while a greedy four leaves two ones.

The reference computes states in increasing amount because every positive coin leads to a smaller amount. For target T and k denominations it uses O(Tk) candidate work and O(T) storage. T is the numeric amount, so a huge value can be expensive even if its decimal input is short. The exercise oracle instead explores reachable amounts with BFS; agreement across small cases is evidence from a different mechanism.

exercise.prompt: Change the stair-count problem to allow moves of one or three steps. Write ways_one_or_three(n) for a nonnegative integer n, using a table where counts[i] is the number of ordered move sequences that reach step i. Start with counts[0]=1; each state adds counts[i-1] and, when i >= 3, counts[i-3].
checks: For n=0 through n=6, the results are 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6; n=4 counts 1+3 and 3+1 separately.
Negative numbers, booleans and non-integers raise ValueError; no negative table index is used to handle the first two steps.

quiz.question: What is essential before writing a DP recurrence?
options: Define the meaning of a state and its base cases
quiz.explanation: State meaning and base cases make the recurrence assessable; recursion is optional.

lessons.title: 12. Linked nodes and ownership
lessons.takeaway: Changing a link changes reachability; finding the link is often the expensive part.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: Model a chain as a node with a value and a next reference. To insert after a known node, first point the new node at the old successor, then point the known node at the new node. Reversing that order can lose the remainder of the chain. Empty lists need an explicit head policy.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: `insert_after` preserves the old successor while inserting a new node. Traversal follows `next` until `None`, producing 1, 2, 3.

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Insertion after an already-known node takes O(1) time. Searching by value takes O(n). The traversal assumes an acyclic chain; a cycle needs a detection policy. A Python list is usually simpler when indexed access and locality matter.

exercise.prompt: Implement removal of the node immediately after a known node, returning its value or None.
exercise.solution:
def remove_after(node):
    victim = node.next
    if victim is None:
        return None
    node.next = victim.next
    return victim.value

assert remove_after(a) == 2
assert values(a) == [1, 3]
checks: Removing a successor preserves the tail.
Removing after the last node returns None.
The sentinel None is ambiguous if None is a valid stored value; document the contract.

quiz.question: Why is insertion by position not necessarily O(1)?
options: The position may need a traversal
quiz.explanation: Only the pointer update is constant-time; locating the node can dominate.

lessons.title: 13. Merge sort and a correctness argument
lessons.takeaway: Merge two sorted runs while preserving the invariant that the output prefix is sorted.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: Divide the input until runs have size zero or one. During merging, the smallest unconsumed value must be at the front of one of the runs. Select that value, advance its pointer, and repeat. Taking from the left on equal keys preserves stability.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: Each recursive call sorts a smaller half. During merging, i and j mark the unconsumed suffixes; choosing the left value on equality preserves stability.

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Each recursion level merges O(n) values, and there are O(log n) levels. Time is O(n log n) under constant-cost comparisons. This copying implementation uses O(n) peak auxiliary storage plus recursion bookkeeping; cumulative allocation is larger. Built-in sorting is preferable in most Python applications.

exercise.prompt: Test sorting against Python's sorted for all permutations of four distinct values.
exercise.solution:
from itertools import permutations
for row in permutations([0, 1, 2, 3]):
    assert merge_sort(row) == sorted(row)
assert merge_sort([]) == []
assert merge_sort([2, 2]) == [2, 2]
checks: All permutations match the oracle.
Input is not modified.
Explain why <= rather than < preserves left-before-right ties.

quiz.question: Why is each merge linear?
options: Each step consumes one remaining value
Both runs are rescanned from zero
quiz.explanation: Each pointer moves forward at most the length of its run.

lessons.title: 14. Quicksort, partitioning and quickselect
lessons.takeaway: Partitioning puts one value in its final place; recursing on both sides sorts, recursing on one side selects.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: Divide and conquer splits a problem, solves the parts and combines the answers. Merge sort does its work in the combine step. Quicksort does it in the split: it partitions around a pivot so smaller values sit to the left and larger values to the right, then sorts each side. Nothing needs combining.
Picking the pivot at random makes bad splits unlikely for any input. Grouping values equal to the pivot, as below, keeps many duplicates from causing deep recursion.
sections.example:
import random

def quicksort(values, rng):
    if len(values) <= 1:
        return list(values)
    pivot = values[rng.randrange(len(values))]
    less = [v for v in values if v < pivot]
    equal = [v for v in values if v == pivot]
    greater = [v for v in values if v > pivot]
    return quicksort(less, rng) + equal + quicksort(greater, rng)

data = [5, 3, 8, 3, 1, 9, 3]
print(quicksort(data, random.Random(7)))
print(data)

# Expected output:
# [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 8, 9]
# [5, 3, 8, 3, 1, 9, 3]

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: In-place quicksort uses a partition with an invariant. Lomuto's scheme keeps `a[lo:p]` below the pivot while `i` scans; a swap extends that region. At the end the pivot moves to index `p`, which is exactly where it belongs in sorted order.

Quickselect reuses partition to find the k-th smallest value. After partitioning, `k` lies on one side only, so it continues there and ignores the other. That is how you find a median or the top k without sorting everything.

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Each partition places one pivot correctly and leaves two independent subproblems, so quicksort is correct by induction on their size. With random pivots the expected cost is O(n log n). If the pivot is always the smallest or largest value, as with a last-element pivot on already sorted input, every split removes one item and the cost becomes O(n²). Recursing into the smaller side first keeps the stack depth O(log n).

Quickselect averages O(n) and has the same quadratic worst case. Quicksort is not stable. No comparison sort can beat O(n log n) in the worst case; counting sort avoids comparisons and runs in O(n + k) when keys are small integers below k. Python's `sorted` uses Timsort, which is stable, O(n log n) and fast on partly sorted data, so write your own sort only to learn or for a special case.
sections.example:
import random

def comparisons(a):
    count = 0
    def sort(lo, hi):
        nonlocal count
        while lo < hi:
            pivot, p = a[hi], lo
            for i in range(lo, hi):
                count += 1
                if a[i] < pivot:
                    a[i], a[p] = a[p], a[i]
                    p += 1
            a[p], a[hi] = a[hi], a[p]
            if p - lo < hi - p:        # recurse into the smaller side
                sort(lo, p - 1)
                lo = p + 1
            else:
                sort(p + 1, hi)
                hi = p - 1
    sort(0, len(a) - 1)
    return count

n = 400
shuffled = list(range(n))
random.Random(1).shuffle(shuffled)
print("already sorted:", comparisons(list(range(n))))
print("shuffled:", comparisons(shuffled))
print("n(n-1)/2 =", n * (n - 1) // 2)

# Expected output:
# already sorted: 79800
# shuffled: 3476
# n(n-1)/2 = 79800

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: Given sorted numbers and a target sum, place pointers at opposite ends. If the sum is too small, increasing the left value is the only useful move; decreasing the right would make it smaller. The symmetric argument applies when the sum is too large.

sections.title: Implementation

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: The sorted-input precondition is essential. Each move shortens the interval, so time is O(n) and extra space O(1). Sorting first costs O(n log n) and changes index meanings unless original indices are carried alongside values.

lessons.title: 16. Prefix sums and bit manipulation
lessons.takeaway: A prefix array answers any range sum with one subtraction; an integer's bits can store a small set and combine sets in one operation.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: A prefix array stores running totals with a leading zero: `prefix[i]` is the sum of the first `i` values. The sum of `values[i:j]` is then `prefix[j] - prefix[i]`, an O(1) answer after an O(n) build. The leading zero removes the special case for ranges that start at 0.

Prefix sums also count subarrays with a target sum when values can be negative, which breaks the sliding window from lesson 17. A range ending here sums to the target exactly when an earlier prefix equals `running - target`, so a Counter of earlier prefixes answers it in one pass. A difference array runs the idea backwards: record each range update at its two ends, then a prefix sum applies all of them.
sections.example:
from collections import Counter
from itertools import accumulate

minutes = [30, 0, 45, 15, 60, 20, 10]
prefix = [0, *accumulate(minutes)]
print(prefix)
print(prefix[5] - prefix[2], sum(minutes[2:5]))

def count_subarrays(values, target):
    seen, running, count = Counter({0: 1}), 0, 0
    for value in values:
        running += value
        count += seen[running - target]
        seen[running] += 1
    return count

print(count_subarrays([3, -1, 4, -3, 2, 1], 3))

def apply_ranges(n, updates):
    diff = [0] * (n + 1)
    for start, stop, amount in updates:  # add amount to positions start..stop-1
        diff[start] += amount
        diff[stop] -= amount
    return list(accumulate(diff[:-1]))

print(apply_ranges(6, [(0, 3, 10), (2, 6, 5)]))

# Expected output:
# [0, 30, 30, 75, 90, 150, 170, 180]
# 120 120
# 6
# [10, 10, 15, 5, 5, 5]

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: An integer can represent a set drawn from a small fixed universe: bit `i` is 1 when item `i` is present. `|` is union, `&` intersection, `^` symmetric difference, and `1 << i` builds a one-item set. Test membership with `mask >> i & 1` and count members with `int.bit_count()`.

`n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so it is 0 exactly for powers of two (and 0 itself). XOR cancels equal values, which finds the one value that appears an odd number of times. Counting from 0 to `2**k - 1` enumerates every subset of k items.
sections.example:
DAYS = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"]

def mask(*days):
    m = 0
    for day in days:
        m |= 1 << DAYS.index(day)
    return m

ada, lin = mask("Mon", "Wed", "Fri"), mask("Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat")
both = ada & lin
print(bin(both), [d for i, d in enumerate(DAYS) if both >> i & 1])
print((ada | lin).bit_count(), ada ^ lin == mask("Mon", "Thu", "Sat"))
print([n for n in [1, 6, 8, 12, 64] if n & (n - 1) == 0])

odd_one = 0
for n in [4, 9, 4, 7, 9]:
    odd_one ^= n
print(odd_one)

items = ["a", "b", "c"]
print([[x for i, x in enumerate(items) if m >> i & 1] for m in range(1 << len(items))])

# Expected output:
# 0b10100 ['Wed', 'Fri']
# 5 True
# [1, 8, 64]
# 7
# [[], ['a'], ['b'], ['a', 'b'], ['c'], ['a', 'c'], ['b', 'c'], ['a', 'b', 'c']]

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Most prefix-sum bugs are off by one. Keep the convention that `prefix` has `n + 1` entries and ranges are half-open, `[i, j)`, and test empty ranges and ranges touching either end. A prefix array is fixed once built; if values change between queries, a Fenwick or segment tree supports updates and range sums in O(log n) each.

Python integers have no fixed width, so shifts never overflow and `~x` is `-x - 1`; in C#, Java or SQL, shifting past the type's width does something else. Use a `set` unless the universe is small and fixed, or you need many fast set operations, as in dynamic programming over subsets with its O(2^n) states.

exercise.prompt: Write answer(values, queries) that returns sum(values[i:j]) for each (i, j) query using one prefix array. Check it against direct sums for 500 random half-open ranges over 100 values that include negatives, including empty ranges, then print the answers for [30, 0, 45, 15] with queries (0, 4), (1, 3) and (2, 2).
exercise.solution:
import random
from itertools import accumulate

def answer(values, queries):
    prefix = [0, *accumulate(values)]
    return [prefix[j] - prefix[i] for i, j in queries]

rng = random.Random(5)
values = [rng.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(100)]
queries = [tuple(sorted((rng.randint(0, 100), rng.randint(0, 100)))) for _ in range(500)]
assert answer(values, queries) == [sum(values[i:j]) for i, j in queries]
print(answer([30, 0, 45, 15], [(0, 4), (1, 3), (2, 2)]))
checks: Output is [90, 45, 0].
The prefix array is built once, not per query.
Ranges that start at 0, end at len(values) or are empty all match the direct sums.

quiz.explanation: prefix[j] totals the first j values and prefix[i] the first i, so their difference is exactly values[i:j].

lessons.title: 17. Sliding windows and maintained state
lessons.takeaway: Maintain the property of a contiguous interval instead of rebuilding every interval.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: Find the longest substring with no repeated characters. Keep the last position of each character and the left edge of the current valid window. On repetition, move left past the prior occurrence only if that occurrence is within the current window.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: last records the most recent index of each character. max prevents left from moving backward when a repeated character lies outside the current window; abba has a longest unique span of length 2.
sections.example:
def longest_unique(text):
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, char in enumerate(text):
        left = max(left, last.get(char, -1) + 1)
        last[char] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

assert longest_unique("abba") == 2

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: The max prevents the left edge moving backward. Expected time O(n) uses hashing assumptions; extra space depends on distinct characters. Python iterates Unicode code points, not user-perceived grapheme clusters. Define the character model for human-language applications.

sections.title: Trace the window before enumerating test inputs
paragraphs: For abba, `right=0` gives a and `left=0`. At `right=1`, ab has length 2. At `right=2`, the prior b at index 1 moves left to 2. At `right=3`, the prior a at 0 lies outside the current window, so left remains 2. Moving left back to 1 would incorrectly accept bba.

The exercise uses `itertools.product("ab", repeat=size)` to generate every tuple of a/b choices of that length. For size 2 those tuples spell aa, ab, ba, bb. Join a tuple into text, then let the slower oracle examine every nonempty substring. The oracle is deliberately easier to check than the optimized window.

quiz.question: Why use max when moving left?
options: To avoid expanding into a previously excluded prefix
quiz.explanation: An older occurrence before the window must not move the boundary backward.

lessons.title: 18. Tries and string search
lessons.takeaway: A trie shares common prefixes so a prefix lookup costs the prefix's length; a rolling hash slides a fingerprint across text and verifies each candidate.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: A trie stores words as paths from the root, one character per edge, with a marker where a word ends. Words with a common prefix share its nodes. Inserting or finding a word of length L takes L steps however many words are stored, and the node at the end of a prefix leads to every word that starts with it, which is what autocomplete needs.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: Checking a pattern of length m at every position of a text of length n costs O(n·m) in the worst case. Rabin–Karp keeps a hash of the current window and updates it in O(1) as the window slides: remove the leftmost character's contribution, shift, add the new character. Only windows whose hash equals the pattern's are compared character by character, because different strings can share a hash.

KMP reaches O(n + m) in every case by precomputing how far the pattern can shift after a mismatch. In everyday Python, `pattern in text`, `str.find` and `re` are already optimized; implement these algorithms to understand them or for special cases such as searching many patterns at once.
sections.example:
def find_all(text, pattern, base=256, mod=1_000_000_007):
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    if m == 0 or m > n:
        return []
    high = pow(base, m - 1, mod)
    target = window = 0
    for i in range(m):
        target = (target * base + ord(pattern[i])) % mod
        window = (window * base + ord(text[i])) % mod
    hits = []
    for start in range(n - m + 1):
        if window == target and text[start:start + m] == pattern:  # verify: hashes can collide
            hits.append(start)
        if start + m < n:
            window = ((window - ord(text[start]) * high) * base + ord(text[start + m])) % mod
    return hits

text = "abracadabra"
print(find_all(text, "abra"))
print([i for i in range(len(text)) if text.startswith("abra", i)])

# Expected output:
# [0, 7]
# [0, 7]

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: A trie trades memory for prefix speed: every node is a dictionary. For a fixed word list, a sorted list with `bisect` finds the block of words with a prefix in O(log n + k) using far less memory. Normalise text before inserting, for example with `casefold()`, or "Sort" and "sort" become different paths.

Rabin–Karp's expected time is O(n + m); many hash collisions push it towards O(n·m), which the final comparison keeps correct but slow. Decide whether matches may overlap: "aa" occurs at 0, 1 and 2 in "aaaa", but `str.count` reports 2 non-overlapping matches.

lessons.title: 19. Dependencies, DFS and topological ordering
lessons.takeaway: A dependency order exists only when the directed graph has no cycle.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: An edge A→B means A must precede B. Kahn's algorithm counts incoming edges, starts with nodes having no remaining prerequisites, then removes their outgoing dependencies. Include nodes appearing only as neighbors in the vertex set.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: indegree counts remaining prerequisites. Each dequeued vertex removes its outgoing constraints; fewer emitted vertices than known vertices indicates a cycle.

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Time and space are O(V+E) and O(V) beyond the input adjacency lists respectively. Multiple valid orders can exist. A DFS alternative uses unseen/active/finished states; encountering an active vertex detects a cycle. Reachability alone does not prove every prerequisite is complete.

sections.title: DFS with a directed cycle witness
paragraphs: Run `directed_dfs` in `trees_graphs.py`. It returns preorder across every component, including isolated and neighbor-only vertices, and a directed cycle witness `[v, ..., v]` or an empty list. White is unseen, gray is on the active path, black is finished. Only an edge to gray proves a directed cycle; an edge to a finished shared prerequisite does not.

An explicit stack retains each adjacency iterator and active-path index. Each vertex/edge is processed once: O(V+E) time and space including normalized adjacency. The tests compare all 512 directed three-vertex graphs with an independent transitive-closure oracle, check witness edges, and cover a 3,000-edge chain without recursion.

from trees_graphs import directed_dfs
assert directed_dfs({'A':['B'],'B':['A']})[1] == ['A','B','A']
assert directed_dfs({'A':['B','C'],'C':['B']})[1] == []

lessons.title: 20. Weighted shortest paths with Dijkstra
lessons.takeaway: A shortest-hop path may not be the minimum-cost path.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: Maintain the best known cost to each vertex. Pop the cheapest candidate from a min-heap; if it is stale, skip it. Relax outgoing edges by proposing a cheaper cost. Nonnegative weights ensure a later detour cannot improve an already settled smallest distance.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: The route A → C → B costs 3 instead of the direct cost 8. Improved distances enter the heap, and stale entries are skipped; a ticket breaks ties without comparing vertex objects.

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Contract: finite nonnegative numeric weights. This lazy-duplicate heap can store O(E) candidates and has O((V+E) log(V+E)) time as a conservative bound, rather than claiming a decrease-key implementation's space bound. The sequence ticket avoids comparing vertex objects on ties.

sections.title: Preconditions versus boundary validation
paragraphs: Finite nonnegative numeric edge weights and hashable vertices in a finite graph are caller preconditions. The teaching implementation checks negative weights, but does not comprehensively validate NaN, infinity, malformed edges or numeric types. Validate these other cases before calling the function with external data.

lessons.title: 21. Union-find and minimum spanning trees
lessons.takeaway: Union-find answers whether two items are already connected in near-constant time, which lets Kruskal's algorithm build a minimum spanning tree from the cheapest edges.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: A disjoint-set (union-find) structure keeps items in groups. Each item points towards a parent, and the root names the group. `find` follows parents to the root; `union` links one root under the other. Two items are connected exactly when they have the same root.

Two rules keep the trees shallow: union by size attaches the smaller tree under the larger, and path halving makes nodes skip a level as `find` walks. Together the amortized cost per operation is almost constant. Groups can merge but never split.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: A minimum spanning tree connects every node of a weighted, undirected graph using the smallest possible total weight. Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges by weight and adds each one unless both ends are already connected; union-find makes that test cheap. A connected graph of n nodes ends with exactly n - 1 edges.

Prim's algorithm grows one tree from a start node, always adding the cheapest edge that leaves it, using a heap as Dijkstra does. Kruskal suits sparse edge lists; Prim suits dense graphs held as adjacency lists.

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Kruskal is correct by the cut property: for any split of the nodes into two sides, the cheapest edge crossing it belongs to some minimum spanning tree. Each edge Kruskal accepts is the cheapest one joining its two current groups. Sorting dominates, so the cost is O(E log E).

A minimum spanning tree minimises the total weight of the network, not the distance between any particular pair; for that, use Dijkstra from lesson 20. Equal weights can give several valid trees with the same total, so tests should compare totals and the edge count rather than one exact edge list. Negative weights are fine here, unlike for Dijkstra.

When its weight is larger than the previous edge's

lessons.title: 22. Greedy algorithms and counterexamples
lessons.takeaway: A locally attractive choice needs a proof, not intuition.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: For unweighted interval scheduling, choose the interval finishing earliest among compatible intervals. Its end leaves at least as much remaining room as another first choice. An exchange argument can replace an optimal solution's first interval with this one without reducing the count.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: Sorting by finish time leaves room for later compatible intervals. The sample chooses three positive-duration intervals; start >= end permits adjacent intervals.

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Each interval must have positive duration: finish > start. Zero-duration and reversed intervals raise `ValueError`. Intervals use half-open boundaries, so one interval may start exactly when another finishes. Empty input returns an empty schedule. Sorting costs O(n log n). Maximizing profit rather than count is a different problem; earliest finish need not maximize total weight. State the objective before selecting a heuristic.

sections.title: Use a small counterexample to reject a tempting rule
paragraphs: Taking the largest coin seems reasonable on 1, 5 and 10, but that observation is not a proof for arbitrary denominations. On 1, 3, 4 with target 6, greedy takes 4+1+1 while 3+3 is better. A counterexample is enough to reject the universal rule; thousands of successful random examples would not prove it.

The supplied method-selection tests keep the failing greedy case as a comparison, not a failing regression. The production answer in that lab is the DP result. Transfer the habit to interval scheduling: a shortest-duration or earliest-start rule needs its own argument, not the proof for earliest finish.

lessons.title: 23. Backtracking with reversible choices
lessons.takeaway: Explore a search tree while restoring state after each choice.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: Generate subsets by deciding whether each input position is included. The recursion state consists of an index and the currently selected values. When returning from the include branch, remove the appended value before exploring another branch.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: Each level explores exclusion and inclusion. The inclusion branch appends an item and then pops it, while a copied selection protects each completed subset.
sections.example:
def subsets(items):
    output, selected = [], []
    def visit(index):
        if index == len(items):
            output.append(selected.copy())
            return
        visit(index + 1)
        selected.append(items[index])
        visit(index + 1)
        selected.pop()
    visit(0)
    return output

assert len(subsets([1,2,3])) == 8

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: There are 2^n subsets; copying each output costs up to n. Output construction therefore costs O(n·2^n), with O(n) recursion state excluding the output. Pruning helps only when a valid condition rules out an entire branch. Duplicate input values may yield duplicate value-subsets.

result[0].append(99)
assert all(99 not in row for row in result[1:])

Empty input returns one empty subset.

options: Copies make an exponential problem linear
quiz.explanation: All outputs would otherwise refer to the same mutable list.

lessons.title: 24. Designing DP states: 0/1 knapsack
lessons.takeaway: Iteration order can determine whether an item is used once or repeatedly.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: Choose a subset of items to maximize total value under an integer capacity. Each item is available once. dp[c] is the best value achievable using processed items at capacity c. Processing capacities downward keeps the current item from using an already-updated state from the same pass.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: Descending capacities ensure each item contributes at most once. Weight 2/value 3 and weight 3/value 4 combine to give value 7 at capacity 5.

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Contract: integer capacity ≥0, positive integer weights and numeric values. Empty selection is permitted. Complexity O(nW) time and O(W) space is pseudo-polynomial: W's numeric value can be large relative to its digit count. Reconstructing the selected items requires additional bookkeeping.

sections.title: Preconditions versus boundary validation
paragraphs: Capacity must be a nonnegative integer and every weight a positive integer; values must be finite numeric values in the stated optimization contract. These are caller preconditions. The function rejects negative capacity and nonpositive weights. Before using external data, also reject fractional capacity or weights, malformed pairs and nonfinite values.

Use `advanced-reasoning.md` and `test_advanced_oracles.py` for the learner extension: explain the invariant and recurrence, run the bounded independent oracles, and test a deliberately wrong implementation.

exercise.prompt: Compare one item of weight 2/value 3 at capacity 4 against the unbounded variant.
exercise.solution:
assert knapsack([(2,3)],4) == 3
assert knapsack([],4) == 0
assert knapsack([(2,3)],0) == 0
# Ascending capacities would reuse the single item and incorrectly return 6.
checks: Single item is used at most once.
Negative-value items can be skipped.
Distinguish state definition, recurrence, order and reconstruction.

quiz.question: Why iterate capacities downward?
options: To avoid reusing the current item
quiz.explanation: dp[c-weight] must still represent only previously processed items.

references.title: Primary reference: Dynamic programming and knapsack
references.scope: Stable algorithm concepts; Python 3.14+ teaching translations. Local exercises are original examples, not source quotations; executable checks listed in task kit.

lessons.title: 25. Testing and reviewing an algorithm
lessons.takeaway: A result, a correctness argument and a complexity claim need separate evidence.

sections.title: Model
paragraphs: For a scheduling or routing project, define the graph/interval model and preconditions first. Implement a simple reference calculation for small inputs, then compare the optimized algorithm with it across generated cases. This finds edge cases without assuming that random success proves correctness.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: The review separates correctness from cost and evidence: establish the contract, invariant and termination, then justify the bound and test against an oracle and adversarial cases.
sections.example:
Review checklist:
Contract → invariant → termination → result correctness
Representation → operations counted → worst-case bound
Tests → oracle → adversarial cases → resource limits

sections.title: Correctness and cost
paragraphs: Benchmarks measure a particular workload and environment. They cannot establish asymptotic complexity by themselves. Separate setup, sorting and parsing from the operation being measured; report input sizes and distributions. Avoid recursive depth claims based on balanced-tree examples alone.

sections.title: Select state and method for a changed constraint
paragraphs: Try a route problem with one optional half-price edge. A location alone is no longer enough state: arriving at B with the discount unused has different future choices from arriving there after spending it. Model (location, `used_discount`), and choose transitions that preserve the resource constraint before selecting a shortest-path method.

This extension is not implemented in `method_selection.py`. A useful concrete case has A→B cost 8, A→C cost 3, C→B cost 3: ordinary cheapest cost is 6, but one half-price edge permits the direct cost 4. Test an unreachable destination and a zero-cost edge too. A passing coin lab does not demonstrate this richer state model.

exercise.prompt: Build a prerequisite planner that detects cycles, returns an order and finds minimum-cost routes on a separate nonnegative weighted graph.
exercise.solution:
Reference architecture:
1. Parse/validate IDs, edges and weights; preserve isolated vertices.
2. Use topological() for dependency ordering; fail on cycles.
3. Use dijkstra() only for the separate cost graph.
4. Validate every returned dependency order against all edges.
5. Test cycles, disconnected vertices, equal-cost routes and zero-cost edges.
6. Record representation-specific cost bounds and reject unsupported inputs.
checks: Keep prerequisite semantics separate from route-cost semantics.
Compare small shortest-path cases with hand calculations or a reference algorithm.
Describe unsupported negative weights and malformed records.
Include an operational size limit and an explanatory error.

quiz.question: Does a fast benchmark prove an O(n) bound?
quiz.explanation: A finite set of timings is empirical evidence, not an asymptotic proof.

references.title: Primary reference: Test cases and assertions
references.scope: Stable algorithm concepts; Python 3.14+ teaching translations. Local exercises are original examples, not source quotations; executable checks listed in task kit.

stages.title: Foundations: representation and cost
stages.description: Choose basic data structures and define their expected results and costs.
exitCriteria: Distinguish a structure's operations from a problem's contract.
Trace arrays, hash tables, stacks and queues by hand.
Explain expected versus worst-case time and auxiliary space.

project.title: Study-event summarizer
project.brief: Process add and undo commands for study events. Build it independently using the concrete contract below.
requirements: An add command supplies a nonempty event ID, topic and nonnegative integer minutes. Inputs meet these shape rules. Count accepted minutes per topic.
Ignore an add whose ID was accepted previously, even if that event was later undone. Undo reverses the most recent still-active accepted add; undo on an empty history does nothing.
Keep a topic in the totals once first accepted, including when its total returns to zero. Preserve caller-owned command data.
For add(a, Python, 20), add(b, SQL, 10), add(a, Python, 99), undo, expect {Python:20, SQL:0}. A second undo gives both totals zero; adding ID a again changes nothing.
Use separate totals, seen IDs and active history. Explain why removing an ID from history does not remove it from the seen set.
rubric: No duplicate is silently counted as a new unique event.
project.solution: Scan commands once. For a new add ID, record the ID permanently, add minutes under its topic and push the accepted event onto a history list. Ignore duplicate IDs without pushing. Undo pops only the active history and subtracts that event's minutes while retaining the topic key. Empty undo is a no-op. This contract counts each ID at most once across the whole command stream, including after undo; it is not redo support.

stages.title: Intermediate: search, traversal and invariants
stages.description: Implement search and traversal algorithms. Check preconditions and loop invariants, and compare small cases with a reference calculation.
exitCriteria: Traverse cyclic graphs safely and detect impossible dependency orders.
Compare optimized results with brute-force results on small inputs.
Account for sorting and copying costs.

project.title: Prerequisite planner
project.brief: Given topics and directed prerequisite edges, produce a valid study order and diagnose cycles.
requirements: Preserve isolated topics and neighbor-only vertices.
Return an order satisfying every dependency or an explicit cycle error.
Use BFS separately to explain reachability, not prerequisite completion.
Test multiple valid orders without asserting one arbitrary sequence.
Document complexity for your chosen representation.
rubric: Every edge is checked against the output order.
Tests cover empty input, one vertex and shared prerequisites.
project.solution: Use Kahn's topological order implementation. Build indegrees for every vertex, enqueue zero-indegree vertices, decrement neighbors and compare output count to vertex count. Validate every returned order by mapping vertices to positions. Keep completion eligibility as a separate check of all prerequisites.

stages.title: Selected advanced practice
stages.description: Test algorithm assumptions, challenge greedy choices with counterexamples, and derive dynamic-programming states.
exitCriteria: Explain why Dijkstra requires nonnegative weights.
Construct a counterexample to an invalid greedy rule.
Define DP state, recurrence, base cases and update order.
Distinguish algorithmic complexity from measured performance.

project.title: Algorithm decision portfolio
project.brief: Implement scheduling, weighted routing and knapsack. Choose an algorithm for each task and test the assumptions it requires.
requirements: Find routes on a nonnegative weighted graph and reject unsupported weights.
Schedule the maximum number of compatible positive-duration unweighted intervals; reject zero-duration and reversed intervals.
Choose items under an integer budget with each item used at most once.
Compare small cases against independent brute-force oracles.
Write invariants, termination arguments and representation-specific complexity.
Define input size limits and document remaining limitations.
rubric: Each task uses the correct objective and preconditions.
Counterexamples explain why plausible alternatives fail.
Tests include ties, duplicates, empty input, rejected nonpositive interval durations, zero-cost edges and disconnected inputs.
Explain which costs are pseudo-polynomial or exponential and what that means for input size.
Results remain correct without performance optimizations.
project.solution: Use lazy-heap Dijkstra for nonnegative costs, earliest-finish greedy for unweighted interval count, and descending-capacity 0/1 knapsack for the budget problem. The advanced_algorithms.py download contains reference functions and checks. Extend it with independent small-input oracles and document why each algorithm applies.
